new_title: England collapse to 87-run defeat by Pakistan in men's tri-series cricket ODI - as it happened
old_text:
44th over: Pakistan 242-6 (Arafat Minhas 32, Faheem Ashraf 25) Back comes Rashid and Faheem continues on his merry way, starting the over with a pair of consecutive thumps to the long-on boundary. Faheem has faced 16 balls and hit five of them for four, which is one more than Babar Azam managed off 52 balls.
43rd over: Pakistan 232-6 (Arafat Minhas 31, Faheem Ashraf 16) Last over for Jacks, too. He thinks he's got Arafat LBW, but the ball was sliding just past the leg stump. Faheem, facing a similar delivery, plays the finest of glances for four, and then goes from artful to agricultural with a swing for four more. Even so, Jacks finishes with 10-0-45-1: he was superb early on.
42nd over: Pakistan 222-6 (Arafat Minhas 31, Faheem Ashraf 7) Overton has reached his last over. He looks for that yorker again but gets it wrong this time, allowing Faheem to play a handsome cover drive. Still, it's been a fine shift from Overton: 10-0-38-1, like something from the 1980s.
41st over: Pakistan 215-6 (Arafat Minhas 30, Faheem Ashraf 2) It's two left-handers at the crease now, so Nasser Hussain wonders if Brook will bring back Jacks with his off-breaks. And he does! It almost works as Arafat flirts with danger by clothing a pull. Four singles off the over.
40th over: Pakistan 211-6 (Arafat Minhas 29, Faheem Ashraf 0) Overton gets some reward at last for his discipline, and Harry Brook gets another tick for keeping him on. It's been an innings of two halves from Pakistan: a trudge to 81-4 off 112 balls before Hasan appeared, a waltz to 130-2 off 128 while he was there.
Well bowled JOverton! After bowling even shorter than before, he switches to the yorker and gets the wicket England most wanted. That's the end of a lovely innings from Hasan, who cruised to 79 off only 74 balls.
39th over: Pakistan 209-5 (Hasan Nawaz 77, Arafat Minhas 29) Arafat, emboldened, spots Curran's moon ball and crunches it over cover for four. Then he plays the best shot of the three, swinging a full ball over mid-on for six, is it - no, four more, but still a statement. And he's not finished yet, as another full ball is drilled past mid-off to make 13 off the over. Second fiddle no longer!
38th over: Pakistan 196-5 (Hasan Nawaz 77, Arafat Minhas 17) Overton, who's been banging away short of a length, bowls a rare half-volley and Arafat cashes in with a whippy on-drive. That's his first four, off the 24th delivery he has faced, but he needn't worry about it because he has helped Hasan add 62 at a run a ball.
37th over: Pakistan 190-5 (Hasan Nawaz 76, Arafat Minhas 12) Good from Curran, who could easily be rusty after his lay-off. He restricts the batters to three singles and very nearly has Arafat caught behind, but it's a tough chance to Jamie Cox's left and he can't quite cling on.
36th over: Pakistan 187-5 (Hasan Nawaz 74, Arafat Minhas 11) When Harry Brook was brave enough to bring Will Jacks on for the seventh over, Pakistan's senior pros weren't brave enough to attack him. Now Jacks comes back and these young batters show how it's done. Hasan hits a handsome cut for four and the other five balls all go for a single. They've added 53 already and look how many of those Arafat has made. Hasan has changed the game.
35th over: Pakistan 178-5 (Hasan Nawaz 67, Arafat Minhas 9) And here is Sam Curran, summoned from the deep at last. He starts as he means to go on, with a super-slow ball. This doesn't please Stuart Broad, who argues that it's not a surprise if the batter hasn't got used to your normal speed. Hasan copes easily enough, waiting several minutes for the ball to arrive, then flicking it round the corner for two as if playing French cricket. He cuts the next ball for two more as England concede an overthrow, before Curran settles down and bowls three dots. Maybe he would tell Broad that slow is his normal speed.
34th over: Pakistan 173-5 (Hasan Nawaz 62, Arafat Minhas 9) Last over with a different ball at each end. Harry Brook is working on one of them, polishing one side in an effort to persuade it to reverse-swing. No sign of that yet but Jamie Overton keeps it tight once again, going for only three singles.
33rd over: Pakistan 170-5 (Hasan Nawaz 60, Arafat Minhas 8) Sometimes the drinks break takes a wicket, and sometimes things continue just as before. Hasan shimmies down the track to hit Rashid's first ball for six, again: he does love to start an over with a statement.
32nd over: Pakistan 161-5 (Hasan Nawaz 52, Arafat Minhas 7) And so to the second drinks break, with Hasan on song but England still on top. It's been a team effort with all the bowlers chipping in - Jacks and Overton with their thrift, Atkinson, Baker and Rashid with wickets, and Curran with two fine catches.
Hasan glides Overton for four to reach the first fifty of the day. He's been more confident than any other batter, more fluent and more entertaining, making 50 off 46 balls with four fours and three sixes.
31st over: Pakistan 154-5 (Hasan Nawaz 46, Arafat Minhas 6) Hasan likes that six so much, he does it again off his next ball, off Rashid. Even with three dots at the end of the over, the partnership is 21 off 21.
30th over: Pakistan 147-5 (Hasan Nawaz 39, Arafat Minhas 6) Pakistan badly need a counter-attack too, and here it comes. The new batter, Arafat, reads Atkinson's length rapidly and cuts him for four well in front of square. Then Hasan flicks him for six! If he can stay in for another 10 overs, his team will still be in the game.
29th over: Pakistan 135-5 (Hasan Nawaz 32, Arafat Minhas 1) Brook, whose brain never sleeps, takes Jacks off (7-0-24-1) and brings back Rashid, who whisks through an over for just two singles.
Meanwhile, at Gqeberha, Marco Jansen has turned into Ian Botham, 1981 vintage.
28th over: Pakistan 133-5 (Hasan Nawaz 31, Arafat Minhas 0) Curran, on his return after injury, has been a specialist fielder so far, but he's still making a difference. Credit too to Harry Brook, who saw Atkinson make a couple of blunders in the deep and gave him a shot at redemption.
WICKET! Saad Baig c Curran b Atkinson 35 (Pakistan 133-5)
The breakthrough! Atkinson's bouncer is spot-on, heading for Saad's face, and although he plays a decent pull, he picks the wrong man to hit it to. Curran races in from deep square to take another assured catch.
27th over: Pakistan 131-4 (Saad Baig 35, Hasan Nawaz 30) Now Hasan is dropped! And again it's Atkinson who lends him a hand, by spilling a simple chance at long leg as Hasan top-edges a sweep off Jacks. The batters run two to bring up a fine 50 partnership off 50 balls. Now they just need to double it.
26th over: Pakistan 128-4 (Saad Baig 34, Hasan Nawaz 28) Pakistan's hopes of a respectable total now rest on Hasan Nawaz, and he's rising to the challenge. He square-drives Baker for what should be two, but Gus Atkinson allows himself to be nutmegged, so it's four. Nawaz rubs it in by backing away to leg and thrashing the next ball for four more, then calms down and plays an artful dab for two. That's 10 off the over, and 35 off the last five.
25th over: Pakistan 118-4 (Saad Baig 34, Hasan Nawaz 18) Ladies and gentlemen, w have a dramatic development: Will Jacks has conceded a four. It comes off the 36th ball he's bowled as Saad Baig clonks him over midwicket. Only two singles off the first five balls, though, and at the halfway stage Harry Brook won't be remotely bothered.
24th over: Pakistan 112-4 (Saad Baig 29, Hasan Nawaz 17) Baker's over goes for five, but only because there are two wides as his bouncers go haywire. A camera goes for a wander above the crowd, which seems a little sparse although there's plenty of hubbub.
23rd over: Pakistan 106-4 (Saad Baig 27, Hasan Nawaz 15) Rashid continues and Saad Baig changes gear, cutting the first ball of the over for two and chipping the last over mid-on for four. These two have added 25 at a run a ball: all Pakistan need now is for them to quadruple it.
22nd over: Pakistan 98-4 (Saad Baig 21, Hasan Nawaz 14) Back comes Sonny Baker, who, if he was a character in a children's book, would be Mr Bustle. Hasan decides to give him the first two balls, settling for defensive pushes, then steps out to whack him past cover for four. Shot!
20th over: Pakistan 92-4 (Saad Baig 20, Hasan Nawaz 9) Saad Baig is playing his second ODI, Hasan Nawaz his sixth, but they already look more comfortable than any other pair of batters today. Nawaz, unlike Salman Agha, is unruffled by Overton's pace, greeting him with a clip for two and a glide for a single. After that, Overton still gets more than his fair share of dots.
19th over: Pakistan 87-4 (Saad Baig 18, Hasan Nawaz 6) In comes Hasan Nawaz with his team in a lot of bother - and he hits his first ball for six! With a lofted on-drive. So it's an expensive over from Rashid, 13 off it, but that's a price worth paying for the scalp of Salman Agha, who made a hundred on Sunday.
18th over: Pakistan 74-3 (Saad Baig 17, Salman Agha 10) Bowling short and fast is often a recipe for runs - cuts, hooks, upper-cuts, top edges over the keeper's head. Not today from Jamie Overton. Salman does get the last ball of the over away for two, but it's an uppish glide that could easily have gone to hand at backward point. Overton has 4-0-8-0.
17th over: Pakistan 70-3 (Saad Baig 17, Salman Agha 7) It's Adil time! Pakistan have been so passive against Jacks that they're going to have to attack England's senior spinner. And Salman does: first ball, down the track, driving over extra-cover, four. By the middle of the over, Adil is all over him like a Rash. This duel is already a good contest.
16th over: Pakistan 65-3 (Saad Baig 17, Salman Agha 2) Overton continues and instantly hits Salman on the hand. Ouch! He gets some treatment and a breather as the umpires take drinks, and he;'s able to continue - but he nearly runs Saad out by going "Yes! No". And Overton, like Jacks, has been allowed to make a miserly start: 3-0-5-0.
15th over: Pakistan 64-3 (Saad Baig 17, Salman Agha 1) Jacks may have bowled that ball a touch faster: Babar, attempting a swat to midwicket, was late on it as it homed in on the off bail. Jacks almost makes it two wickets in two balls as Salman Agha plays a straight chip and flirts with a caught-and-bowled. Saad Baig, who has worked out that he'll have to be the grown-up in the room, cuts the last ball of the over for four. But Jacks' figures are still outstanding: 5-0-15-1.
And now he's gone! Babar misses a straight one, for reasons that are hard to fathom - but it's just deserts for Jacks' accuracy, and for Babar's lassitude.
14th over: Pakistan 58-2 (Babar Azam 34, Saad Baig 12) Babar, meanwhile, is threatening to be the junior partner to a 19-year-old. He does manage a clip for two off JOverton.
13th over: Pakistan 54-2 (Babar Azam 31, Saad Baig 12) Three singles off Jacks, who has, I'm fairly sure, not conceded a two, let alone a four. His four overs have gone for just nine runs, a bonus for England as he's very much the junior partner to Adil Rashid.
12th over: Pakistan 51-2 (Babar Azam 29, Saad Baig 11) Atkinson gets a breather after a solid opening spell (5-0-22-1). On comes Jamie Overton, the Liam Plunkett of this team, to bang it in and stick it up 'em. He duly surprises Saad Baig with his pace and bounce, beating him outside off with a ball clocked at 88mph, and this is yet another over that goes for just one run.
11th over: Pakistan 50-2 (Babar Azam 28, Saad Baig 11) As Jacks continues, the batters finally begin to milk him. They take four singles, but one is off the edge as Jacks' angle, from round the wicket, bothers Babar.
"Hi Tim," says Nick Terdre, "Looks like the 9am start caught you out!" Guilty as charged. "Apart from Sam Curran, who is in the England team?" That's one thing I have managed to cover: see 7th over.
10th over: Pakistan 46-2 (Babar Azam 26, Saad Baig 9) Saad Baig is 19, keeping wicket, making his second international appearance - and now, after a tongue-tied start, he suddenly finds his voice. He glides Atkinson for four, with a hint of edge, then cover-drives for four more with conviction.
9th over: Pakistan 34-2 (Babar Azam 25, Saad Baig 0) Jacks continues, so he wasn't just a ploy for the quicks to swap round... and again he does well. This partnership is spoiling us: 19 balls used up, three runs scored.
8th over: Pakistan 33-2 (Babar Azam 24, Saad Baig 0) Brook takes Baker off, wicket or no wicket, to allow Gus Atkinson to change ends, which may explain why Jacks got that early go. Just a single off this over too: Babar seems to be back to form.
7th over: Pakistan 32-2 (Babar Azam 23, Saad Baig 0) Brook makes his first bowling change and springs a surprise by turning to Will Jacks' off-breaks, rather than Sam Curran's slow-ball allsorts. Jacks is on the money, conceding only a single.
That England team in full: Duckett, Banton, Root, Brook, Cox (wkt), Curran, Jacks, Overton, Atkinson, Rashid, Baker. No Jofra Archer as he's been rested for this tour, and rightly so after a hectic year.
6th over: Pakistan 31-2 (Babar Azam 22, Saad Baig 0) Saim had just hit Baker for four - but only off the edge, through a vacant cordon. Harry Brook brings a slip in for the new batter's first ball. Baker has been expensive (3-0-20-1) but, as usual, he's made things happen.
5th over: Pakistan 26-1 (Babar Azam 21, Saim Ayub 4) So sorry for the delay - nobody's fault but mine. England didn't help by taking a wicket with their first ball, as Gus Atkinson lured Fakhar Zaman into a loose clip to Joe Root at midwicket. That prompted Babar Azam to change the habit of a lifetime and get off to a quick start.
Morning everyone. Or should that be welcome back, my friends, to the show that never ends? Three weeks and two days after the last hurrah of the international summer, England are in action on the first of their five winter tours.
That day at the Oval, England were unstoppable, piling up 355 and then bowling Sri Lanka out for 132, which was barely any more than Tom Banton had made off his own bat. Will Banton, Harry Brook, Jordan Cox, Gus Atkinson and Liam Dawson still be in top form now? It's anyone's guess. In cricket, the picture can change in the space of a drinks break.
England have some momentum under Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum after beating India as well as Sri Lanka in the summer. But Brook's record as an ODI captain away from home is modest: won 2, lost 4. And Pakistan started this tri-series with a win on Sunday, as Salman Agha continued his soap opera by making a hundred and the Sri Lankan tail wilted in the face of Pakistan's fast bowlers. That game, like this one, was in Rawalpindi, which tends to offer pace and bounce.
England have played only three ODIs in Pakistan in the past 21 years - all early last year, all in the Champions Trophy, and all ending in defeat. The last time they met Pakistan in a 50-over game on Pakistani soil was at Rawalpindi in 2005, when England, captained by Marcus Trescothick, won a low-scoring tussle by six runs, thanks to four wickets from Jimmy Anderson and three from Ian Blackwell. England's other spinner on that occasion was Shaun Udal. It would be another four years before they called up Adil Rashid, who now seems to have been there forever.
This is a day-nighter with play starting at 2pm in Rawalpindi, 10am BST. I'll be back with the toss and the teams 25 minutes before that. In the meantime, here's a perceptive series preview from Taha Hashim.
new_text:
After the embarrassment of their English summer this was a welcome sight for Pakistan. A contest in front of their own, no Ollie Robinson to wobble down a lethal Dukes ball, and a format they are far more comfortable with. The result was an impressive victory against England, who fell 87 runs short in their first match of this one-day international tri-series.
At the centre was Arafat Minhas, playing only his fifth ODI but already making a serious splash, finishing with astounding figures of six for 40. Oh, and he can bat too. The 21-year-old began with a half-century from No 7, resuscitating Pakistan's innings alongside another newcomer, Hasan Nawaz, as 81 for four turned into a total of 302.
Minhas' left-arm spin was next, and he accounted for Harry Brook with a magical delivery as England crumbled, a decent position of 165 for three turning into 215 all out. Minhas was the closer, showing off another skill: he pulled off a direct hit to run out Gus Atkinson and end the game with 11.2 overs left.
[On the partnership between Hasan Nawaz and Arafat Minhas] It's a good sign for us but we also need more runs from our top order.
[On Arafat's player-of-the-match performance] He's a very good talent, a proper allrounder. It's good for us and hopefully he'll deliver in many more games.
We were happy chasing 300 and thought their total was slightly under-par.
Banton and Ducky set the tone beautifully but we lost too many wickets in clumps and couldn't string any partnerships together.
We've spoken a lot about rotation of strike in the middle. Today I thought we were probably too careful against the spinners; we can put them under more pressure.
England's collapse was not entrely pretty. They were 91 for 0, then 165 for 3, but it was all a bit of strain from the moment Harry Brook was bowled by Arafat.
Arafat Minhas, playing only his fifth ODI at the age of 21, hit 59 from 58 balls and then turned the game in a remarkable spell of left-arm bowling. His final figures were 8.4-0-40-6.
As for England, erm... we'll get back to you on that.
Sonny Baker defended the hat-trick ball, then turned Arafat off the pads for a single. Atkinson wanted two and was four-fifths of the way down the pitch when Baker sent him back. Arafat fumbled an awkward throw, but had time to retrieve the ball and detonate the stumps with Atkinson still well short.
Make that six wickets! Arafat is on a hat-trick after trapping Rashid LBW with a classic arm ball. Rashid pushed down the wrong line and was hit on the kneeroll. He reviewed to no avail.
WICKET! England 214-8 (Jacks c Afridi b Arafat 19)
Five wickets for Arafat Minhas! What a performance from a richly talented young cricketer. Jacks hammers a pull straight to midwicket and is caught by Afridi, a carbon copy of Banton's dismissal earlier in the day.
38th over: England 214-7 (Jacks 19, Atkinson 7) A nice stroke from Atkinson, a short-arm pull for four off Afridi. Eight from the over, a decent one for England. But they are a long way behind the game now.
"Come on Rob, this is England, it's not over yet!" says Simon McMahon. "And even if it is, Joburg in 13 months, Anderson with 4-40 and Stokes to hit the winning runs in the final, dreams are free, eh..?"
37th over: England 206-7 (Jacks 17, Atkinson 1) Arafat Minhas, 21 years old, is having a day-night to remember: he helped rescue Pakistan with 59 from 58 balls and now has figures of 8-0-39-4. When he came onto bowl, England seemed to be strolling to victory.
Another wicket would give Arafat two five-fors in only five ODIs; he took one on debut against Australia on this ground in May.
Arafat Minhas gets his fourth wicket! Jamie Overton, who has such a poor record against spin, chips tamely to long on and stomps off the field. "It's appalling batting," says Stuart Broad on Sky.
35th over: England 197-6 (Jacks 10, Overton 0) Barring an unlikely twist, this will be the second time in three ODIs that England have lost when chasing 300+. That can happen to any team; the concern for England is that on both occasions they had a perfect start, only to stick their size 11s in the quicksand.
Cox pulls Arafat serenely for six, one foot in the air as he skips back in his crease - but Arafat's revenge is a dish served piping hot. Three balls later, Cox misses a whip to leg and is plumb LBW. He takes a review with him as well.
That was a lovely piece of bowling from Arafat. Cox thought he could get to it as he lunged forward; he was wrong and it skidded on to hit the pad.
34th over: England 188-5 (Cox 11, Jacks 8) Haris Rauf, who has already bounced out Duckett and Curran, tries to do the same to Jacks. No dice, soldier: Jacks hooks an empathic six over fine leg.
Jacks then drags a pull onto his thigh. That kept a bit low and could easily have flown back onto the stumps.
Time for Pakistan to choose which ball they want to use for the remainder of the innings. England need 115 from 96 balls.
33rd over: England 180-5 (Cox 10, Jacks 1) England have some hitters to come, but these are the last proper batters. Jacks gets off the mark with a single from his sixth ball.
England seemed to be cruising when they were 117 for 1 after 18 overs. Since then they've scored 62 for 4 in 15 overs. Arafat changed the mood and now the quick bowlers are running with it.
32nd over: England 177-5 (Cox 8, Jacks 0) Waqar Younis thinks the ball that got Curran stopped in the pitch, which is why he didn't go through with the stroke as intended. Either way, he's gone and England are in trouble after a terrific over from Haris Rauf: one run, one wicket.
Pakistan review for LBW against Jacks! Haris Rauf has bounced out both England's left-handers. He wants a right-hander, too, and goes up for LBW when Jacks misses a pull at a ball that keeps low. Missing leg, I think, but Pakistan have reviewed.
Pakistan are favourites now! Curran shakes his head after pulling Haris Rauf straight to deep backward square, where the substitute Ghazi Ghori takes a well-judged catch. Curran didn't fully commit to the pull and will be lamenting that particular life choice as he walks off the field. It was a scruffy innings: 27 from 39 balls with no fours and one six.
31st over: England 175-4 (Curran 27, Cox 6) Cox's first boundary is a beauty, threaded between mid off and extra cover off the bowling of Naseem. He tries another drive, this one a bit more handsy, and is beaten. This is fascinating stuff - I'd make Pakistan slight favourites, but William Goldman knows more about this stuff than me.
"Afternoon Rob," says Simon McMahon. "The late-career renaissance must be incredibly satisfying (I'm still waiting, but we live in hope, right..?) George Foreman springs to mind, and Watson at the 2009 Open Nicklaus at the 86 Masters, Bristow 1997. There must be many others that I'm sure the OBO hive mind will uncover. Graham Gooch? Doug Mountjoy?"
They probably achieved more in the early part of their careers than Tom Banton (and Damien Martyn), but I'm not going to debate you, Jerry argue about it with you on the information superhighway.
30th over: England 170-4 (Curran 26, Cox 2) Those loose strokes from Duckett and especially Banton look more costly now. Arafat changes ends to replace Saim and concedes five singles. "It's about milking," says Waqar Younis, "for the next few overs."
This is beautifully poised; England need 133 from 120 balls.
29th over: England 165-4 (Curran 23, Cox 0) Replays show that Root bottom-edged that ball from Naseem onto the stumps - but it definitely kept low and there may have been a hint of reverse swing as well.
After 11 consecutive overs of spin, Naseem Shah returns to the attack and takes the big wicket straight away! Root didn't have much chance with a quick, straight delivery that kept low and pegged back the off stump. As a wise man once said, pace is pace.
28th over: England 164-3 (Root 33, Curran 22) It looks like Pakistan are trying to use up as many overs as spin as possible before the dew becomes a factor. Saim is reverse swept for two by Root in an over that costs five.
27th over: England 159-3 (Root 30, Curran 20) Another tidy over from Arafat, who has good figures of 5-0-19-2 to go with his 58-ball 59 earlier in the day.
26th over: England 156-3 (Root 30, Curran 17) A stinker of a delivery from Saim is pulled mightily over midwicket for six by Curran. That's a much needed boundary, England's first since the 18th over. Saim will be frustrated - he's been pretty accurate, but that was begging to be spanked.
On Sky Sports, Urooj Mumtaz thinks the dew should start to take effect in the next 20 or 30 minutes. That usually makes batting under lights much easier.
25th over: England 147-3 (Root 28, Curran 8) Curran tries to cut the impressive Arafat and is beaten. He's made a scratchy start, certainly in comparison to Root, but we know he is very good at catching up in white-ball cricket.
Three from the over. Pakistan have turned the screw since the bonus wicket of Banton.
24th over: England 144-3 (Root 28, Curran 7) For the second consecutive over, Saim Ayub concedes only four singles. He's doing a useful job with his occasional offspin, eating up overs and gently pushing up the required rate. It's now 6.11, or 159 runs from 156 balls.
23rd over: England 140-3 (Root 26, Curran 5) Root reverse sweeps Arafat deftly for three. England's last boundary was in the 18th over but that shouldn't trouble Root and Curran at this stage. Root has 26 from 22 balls, Curran 5 from 10.
"Using the OBO to follow while at work, writes Michael Duggan. "But until Brook was out it seemed a routine chase. Spin makes it more interesting - as it always does."
22nd over: England 135-3 (Root 22, Curran 4) Low-risk cricket from Root and Curran, who take two singles apiece from Saim's fifth over. England can't afford to lose another quick wicket; conversely, Pakistan must be tempted to bring back one of their quick bowlers at this end.
"Afternoon Rob, afternoon everyone," wrote Eddy Nason about 10 minutes ago. "Root and Brook at the crease, and I should feel comfortable in two of the worlds best batters occupying the crease for England, but this is Pakistan - it all feels like a trap..."
Eddy has just followed up: "So I guess it was a quickfire trap."
21st over: England 131-3 (Root 20, Curran 2) Sam Curran has been promoted to No5, mainly to give England a left/right combination. He's also a good man to have around in a mini-crisis.
Brook is bowled by a beauty! Arafat has changed the mood of the match by striking twice in his first two overs. Brook misread the length and was back when he should have been forward. But it was a superb delivery from around the wicket that straightened sharply to hit the top of off and middle. There's a game on here all right.
20th over: England 125-2 (Root 18, Brook 5) England milk Saim for six, none in boundaries. The required rate isn't an issue so they can afford to play themselves in.
WICKET! England 120-2 (Banton c Afridi b Arafat 57)
The left-arm spinner Arafat Minhas strikes third ball! Banton slugs a short ball straight to midwicket and leans on his bat in disbelief. It was a smart catch from Afridi, but Banton knows he should have hit the ball either straight down or over the top. Eventually he drags himself from the field, all the while lamenting the runs he has left out there. Banton made 57 from 53 balls and, in the parlance of 2009, looked the goods.
18th over: England 117-1 (Banton 55, Root 15) Root glides Saim for four - a trademark shot, beautifully played. England score off every delivery, with 10 coming from the over. They're in a terrific position here, though it's worth remembering that they were 143 for 0 chasing 326 v Sri Lanka and lost.
17th over: England 107-1 (Banton 51, Root 9) The required rate is loitering around a run a ball, which means Root can play at his natural tempo. That includes helping himself to a boundary when Rauf bowls a short ball on the hip. Nice shot, mind, placed deliberately fine to beat the man on the boundary.
Things can change quickly, especially when these two play each other, but right now England are cruising.
16th over: England 101-1 (Banton 50, Root 4) Banton cuts Ayub for two to reach another confident fifty: 46 balls, five fours, two sixes. Top Bantz indeed.
15th over: England 96-1 (Banton 48, Root 1) Banton moves closer to another fifty with a gorgeous stroke, an on-drive for four off Rauf. He was 6 not out from 16 balls; he's now 48 from 43.
"Whisper it, Rob, but is Tom Banton the opener we've been looking for all along for ODI cricket?" says Guy Hornsby "I know he's been around for ever, but at 27 he appears to be in his cricketing prime. It's easy to forget he was barely into his twenties when he debuted in white-ball cricket, but it feels so triumphant when a player struggles early on then comes back mid-career. A small sample size, even more so up top, but averaging 42 at a strike rate north of 100 in 50-over cricket is exciting, even if it's only me."
Permission to be really boring and say it's too early to judge? I like the way he complements Duckett, mind, and he plays some belting strokes. I'm also with you on the charm of players excelling in their second career. Damien Martyn - who missed six years of Test cricket because of one poor shot - is one of my favourite examples.
Time after time, Haris Rauf makes something happen. He has made the breakthrough with a good bouncer that Duckett top-edged straight to Fakhar Zaman at fine leg. A frustrated Duckett goes for a breezy 45.
14th over: England 88-0 (Banton 43, Duckett 43) Saim Ayub is the first spinner into the attack. Ben Duckett is having a reasonably animated chat with the umpires about something; what, I know not.
No turn for Ayub but he starts economically: three dot balls, two singles, one two.
13th over: England 84-0 (Banton 42, Duckett 40) England planned to invest in an opening partnership of Ben Duckett and Jacob Bethell. Then Bethell got injured, Tom Banton moved up the order and now all bets are off. It's a small sample size - three and a bit games - but as an opener Banton is averaging 83 and has a strike rate of 117.

"Moving on to less contentious ground, do you subscribe to the view that ODI tactics are changing in the last year or so with the advent of swapping back to a single white ball after the 34 over mark?" asks Lord Baron, sorry Brian Withington. "Apparently only Ireland, India and England have maintained run rates in the latter stages over the relevant period, which have seen marked increases in reverse swing. I am not sure the number of games played under new conditions yet meets the requirements of statistical significance yet, so your thoughts would be even more valuable than usual, he insinuated winningly."
Arf. I haven't buried myself in the numbers - that's in the diary for Friday evening - but from what I've seen it's been a triumph. Don't take my word for it: Mike Atherton, whose thoughts really are valuable, has beenn full of praise for it on the Sky Sports podcast.

Three weeks and two days after the last hurrah of the international summer, England are in action on the first of their five winter tours. That day at the Oval, England were unstoppable, piling up 355 and then bowling Sri Lanka out for 132, which was barely any more than Tom Banton had made off his own bat. Will Banton, Harry Brook, Jordan Cox, Gus Atkinson and Liam Dawson still be in top form now? It's anyone's guess. In cricket, the picture can change in the space of a drinks break. England have some momentum under Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum after beating India as well as Sri Lanka in the summer. But Brook's record as an ODI captain away from home is modest: won 2, lost 4. And Pakistan started this tri-series with a win on Sunday, as Salman Agha continued his soap opera by making a hundred and the Sri Lankan tail wilted in the face of Pakistan's fast bowlers. That game, like this one, was in Rawalpindi, which tends to offer pace and bounce. England have played only three ODIs in Pakistan in the past 21 years - all early last year, all in the Champions Trophy, and all ending in defeat. The last time they met Pakistan in a 50-over game on Pakistani soil was at Rawalpindi in 2005, when England, captained by Marcus Trescothick, won a low-scoring tussle by six runs, thanks to four wickets from Jimmy Anderson and three from Ian Blackwell. England's other spinner on that occasion was Shaun Udal. It would be another four years before they called up Adil Rashid, who now seems to have been there forever.
